questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and long-standing ascites presents with low-grade fever and diffuse abdominal discomfort. Diagnostic paracentesis is performed, and the ascitic fluid is sent for cell count and culture. Which ascitic fluid finding is diagnostic of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) even if the culture is ultimately negative?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear (PMN) count of at least 250 cells/mm3

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ascitic fluid total protein above 3 g/dL

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ascitic fluid lactate dehydrogenase above serum level

explanation.summary: SBP is diagnosed by an elevated ascitic PMN count regardless of culture results.
explanation.whyCorrect: An ascitic fluid PMN count of at least 250 cells/mm3 is the established diagnostic threshold for SBP and prompts empiric therapy even when cultures are negative (culture-negative neutrocytic ascites).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Low ascitic glucose can be seen in secondary peritonitis but is not the diagnostic criterion for SBP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Elevated ascitic amylase suggests pancreatic ascites or bowel perforation, not SBP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: High ascitic protein actually argues against uncomplicated cirrhotic ascites and is not a diagnostic criterion for SBP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Elevated ascitic LDH is one of Runyon's criteria suggesting secondary peritonitis, not the diagnostic threshold for SBP.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman with cirrhosis is diagnosed with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis after paracentesis reveals 800 PMNs/mm3. Ascitic fluid culture is sent. Which single organism is the most likely cause of her infection?

explanation.summary: SBP is usually monomicrobial and caused by enteric gram-negative rods, most often E. coli.
explanation.whyCorrect: E. coli is the single most common cause of SBP, reflecting translocation of enteric gram-negative flora across the gut wall; Klebsiella and streptococci follow.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacteroides fragilis is an anaerobe typical of polymicrobial secondary peritonitis, not monomicrobial SBP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Staphylococcus epidermidis is characteristic of dialysis-catheter-associated peritonitis, not SBP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Candida albicans is a fungal cause seen in dialysis or tertiary peritonitis, not typical SBP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: C. difficile causes colitis, not spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with 12 hours of severe, constant abdominal pain. He lies motionless on the stretcher and winces when the bed is bumped. On examination the abdomen is rigid with involuntary guarding. Which single examination finding is the MOST specific for peritoneal inflammation?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Periumbilical pain radiating to the back

explanation.summary: Involuntary rigidity is the most specific sign of peritonitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inflammation of the parietal peritoneum triggers a spinal reflex arc producing involuntary muscle contraction (rigidity) that the patient cannot relax, making it the most specific physical sign of peritonitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Distention is nonspecific and occurs with ileus, obstruction, and ascites without peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fever is a sensitive but nonspecific sign of infection generally.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bowel sounds are typically diminished or absent (ileus) in peritonitis, not hyperactive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: That pain pattern suggests pancreatitis or aortic pathology, not a specific sign of peritoneal irritation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old patient on continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis (CAPD) notices that the fluid draining from the catheter has become cloudy over the past day and reports mild abdominal pain. Which mechanism best explains how this type of peritonitis typically develops?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial translocation across an intact intestinal wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hematogenous seeding from a distant pneumonia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perforation of a hollow viscus with spillage of enteric contents

choices.label: D
choices.text: Entry of skin flora into the peritoneum through or around the dialysis catheter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Metastatic tumor implantation on the peritoneal surfaces

explanation.summary: Dialysis-associated peritonitis results from skin organisms entering via the catheter.
explanation.whyCorrect: In peritoneal dialysis peritonitis, bacteria (commonly skin flora such as Staphylococcus epidermidis or S. aureus) gain access to the peritoneal cavity through or alongside the indwelling catheter, producing cloudy effluent.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Translocation across an intact gut wall is the mechanism of SBP in cirrhotic ascites, not catheter-associated peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hematogenous spread is an uncommon route and not the typical mechanism in a dialysis patient with a catheter.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Viscus perforation causes secondary peritonitis, a different category with polymicrobial flora.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor implantation causes peritoneal carcinomatosis, not infectious dialysis peritonitis.

questions.stem: A cirrhotic patient is diagnosed with uncomplicated spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. The team plans management. Which of the following best describes the appropriate treatment approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Emergent exploratory laparotomy for source control

choices.label: D
choices.text: Percutaneous drain placement into the ascites collection

explanation.summary: SBP is treated medically with a third-generation cephalosporin and no surgery.
explanation.whyCorrect: SBP has no surgical source, so it is managed with antibiotics alone; a third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime or ceftriaxone) is standard empiric therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Laparotomy is reserved for secondary peritonitis with a perforation; SBP has no source to control.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Broad-spectrum antibiotics plus surgery describes secondary peritonitis management, not SBP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fungal coverage is not appropriate for typical bacterial SBP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Draining the ascites does not treat SBP and is not indicated; antibiotics are the treatment.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with cirrhosis is admitted for presumed SBP and started on cefotaxime. He deteriorates over 24 hours with hypotension, and the ascitic culture grows E. coli, Enterococcus, and Bacteroides fragilis. Repeat paracentesis shows a PMN count of 9,000/mm3 with low glucose. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continue cefotaxime alone and reassess in 48 hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: Broaden antibiotics and obtain urgent imaging and surgical evaluation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discontinue antibiotics because the culture is contaminated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Add intraperitoneal vancomycin through a dialysis catheter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start large-volume paracentesis with albumin as definitive therapy

explanation.summary: Polymicrobial growth with clinical deterioration indicates secondary peritonitis requiring source control.
explanation.whyCorrect: A polymicrobial culture, very high PMN count, low glucose, and failure to improve on cefotaxime point to secondary peritonitis from a perforated viscus; management requires broadening antibiotics and urgent imaging/surgery for source control.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Continuing narrow therapy ignores the evidence of secondary peritonitis and a probable perforation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Multiple enteric species with a high PMN count is not contamination; it signals a surgical source.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This patient has no dialysis catheter; intraperitoneal antibiotics apply to CAPD peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Large-volume paracentesis treats tense ascites, not the underlying perforation and infection.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with acute abdominal pain and free air under the diaphragm on upright chest radiograph, consistent with a perforated colonic diverticulum. He is taken toward the operating room. Which empiric antibiotic regimen best matches the expected microbiology of his peritonitis?

explanation.summary: Secondary peritonitis needs broad coverage of gram-negatives, anaerobes, and enterococci.
explanation.whyCorrect: A perforated colon spills polymicrobial flora, so empiric therapy must cover enteric gram-negative rods, anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis), and enterococci; piperacillin/tazobactam provides this breadth, alongside surgical source control.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cefotaxime alone lacks reliable anaerobic and enterococcal coverage needed for secondary peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral ciprofloxacin is inadequate for a critically contaminated abdomen and lacks anaerobic coverage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intraperitoneal antibiotics are used for dialysis peritonitis, not surgical secondary peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fungal monotherapy does not address the dominant bacterial flora of a perforated viscus.

questions.stem: A patient describes their abdominal pain as beginning several hours ago as a vague, dull discomfort around the umbilicus that was hard to pinpoint, but is now sharp, constant, and localized to a single spot that worsens when they cough or shift position. Which statement best explains this evolution of pain?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Visceral pain is always sharp and localized from onset

choices.label: B
choices.text: The change indicates resolution of the underlying inflammation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dull midline visceral pain becomes sharp and localized once the parietal peritoneum is involved

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parietal peritoneal fibers are autonomic and produce poorly localized pain

choices.label: E
choices.text: The parietal peritoneum lacks innervation and cannot generate pain

explanation.summary: Pain migrates from dull visceral to sharp somatic as parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early visceral pain from the organ is dull, midline, and poorly localized; when inflammation reaches the richly somatically innervated parietal peritoneum, pain becomes sharp, well-localized, and aggravated by movement.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Visceral pain is characteristically dull and poorly localized, not sharp from onset.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Progression to sharp localized pain signals worsening peritoneal irritation, not resolution.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Parietal peritoneal fibers are somatic and produce well-localized pain, not poorly localized autonomic pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The parietal peritoneum is richly innervated with somatic fibers and is the source of localized pain.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with a history of ovarian carcinoma presents with abdominal distention. CT shows nodular thickening and 'caking' of the omentum with diffuse implants studding the peritoneal surfaces and malignant-appearing ascites. Which process best describes these findings?

explanation.summary: Diffuse metastatic seeding of the peritoneum with omental caking is carcinomatosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peritoneal carcinomatosis is metastatic spread of cancer (classically ovarian) onto peritoneal surfaces, producing omental caking, serosal implants, and malignant ascites.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SBP is an infection of cirrhotic ascites, not tumor implants with omental caking.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pseudomyxoma peritonei produces gelatinous mucinous ascites from an appendiceal tumor, not discrete omental caking from ovarian cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mesothelioma is a primary asbestos-related mesothelial malignancy, not metastatic seeding from a known ovarian primary.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tertiary peritonitis is persistent/recurrent infection after treated secondary peritonitis, not a malignant process.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with a remote history of occupational asbestos exposure presents with abdominal distention and ascites. Peritoneal biopsy shows a tumor of mesothelial origin. Which immunohistochemical profile best supports peritoneal mesothelioma over metastatic adenocarcinoma?

explanation.summary: Mesothelioma stains calretinin-positive and CEA-negative.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peritoneal mesothelioma expresses mesothelial markers such as calretinin and is negative for CEA, which distinguishes it from CEA-positive metastatic adenocarcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is the reverse pattern and is characteristic of adenocarcinoma, not mesothelioma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD117 positivity suggests a GIST, not mesothelioma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chromogranin and synaptophysin mark neuroendocrine tumors, not mesothelioma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CDX2 marks intestinal adenocarcinoma, not mesothelioma.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman undergoes surgery for a suspected ruptured appendix and is found to have the abdominal cavity filled with abundant gelatinous, mucinous material coating the peritoneal surfaces. Pathology of the appendix reveals a mucinous neoplasm. Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

explanation.summary: Gelatinous mucinous ascites from a mucinous appendiceal neoplasm is pseudomyxoma peritonei.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pseudomyxoma peritonei ('jelly belly') is progressive accumulation of mucinous ascites, almost always from a ruptured mucinous appendiceal neoplasm spreading mucin-producing cells over peritoneal surfaces.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mesothelioma is a solid mesothelial malignancy linked to asbestos, not gelatinous mucin from the appendix.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SBP produces cloudy infected ascites in cirrhosis, not gelatinous mucin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ovarian carcinomatosis produces solid implants and malignant ascites, not the classic mucinous 'jelly belly' from an appendiceal primary.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dialysis peritonitis is an infection via a catheter, unrelated to mucinous appendiceal tumor.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man on CAPD develops cloudy dialysate and abdominal pain. Effluent cell count is elevated with a neutrophil predominance, and Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which organism is the most likely cause?

explanation.summary: Dialysis peritonitis is most often caused by gram-positive skin flora entering via the catheter.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gram-positive cocci in clusters and cloudy effluent in a CAPD patient point to skin flora such as coagulase-negative staphylococci (S. epidermidis) or S. aureus, the most common causes of dialysis peritonitis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: E. coli is a gram-negative rod and the classic cause of SBP, not the gram-positive cluster organism seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bacteroides fragilis is an anaerobic gram-negative rod typical of secondary peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S. pneumoniae are gram-positive cocci in pairs/chains, not clusters, and is not the most common dialysis pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pseudomonas is a gram-negative rod and a less common, more virulent dialysis pathogen, not matching the Gram stain.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man with ascites is evaluated for peritonitis. The team wishes to distinguish spontaneous bacterial peritonitis from secondary peritonitis due to a perforated viscus. Which examination or fluid finding most strongly favors secondary peritonitis over SBP?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Involuntary rigidity of the abdominal wall

choices.label: E
choices.text: A single organism on ascitic culture

explanation.summary: True rigidity in an ascites patient suggests secondary, not spontaneous, peritonitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: SBP rarely produces true involuntary rigidity; when rigidity is present in a patient with ascites, it raises concern for secondary peritonitis from a perforated viscus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fever and tachycardia occur in both SBP and secondary peritonitis and do not discriminate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Generalized tenderness is common to both and is nonspecific.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cloudy fluid reflects a high cell count seen in SBP as well, so it does not distinguish the two.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A single (monomicrobial) organism actually favors SBP; polymicrobial growth favors secondary peritonitis.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man presents with sudden, severe, diffuse abdominal pain and a rigid abdomen. The clinician suspects a perforated peptic ulcer with free intraperitoneal air. Which initial imaging study is the classic, rapid test for detecting free air under the diaphragm?

explanation.summary: An upright chest radiograph classically detects free subdiaphragmatic air from perforation.
explanation.whyCorrect: An upright chest radiograph is particularly useful for demonstrating free intraperitoneal air collecting under the diaphragm, a hallmark of hollow viscus perforation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ultrasound is operator-dependent and poor at demonstrating small amounts of free air under the diaphragm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A supine film is far less sensitive for free air than an upright view, where air rises under the diaphragm.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MRCP evaluates the biliary/pancreatic ducts, not free peritoneal air, and is slow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A tagged-WBC scan localizes occult infection over hours and is not the rapid test for free air.

questions.stem: A medical student asks why a patient with generalized peritonitis lies perfectly still and resists any movement, in contrast to a patient with a ureteral stone who paces and writhes. Which explanation is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Peritonitis pain is colicky and relieved by changing position

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ureteral stones cause peritoneal rigidity that forces the patient to lie still

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peritonitis patients are typically hypovolemic and too weak to move

choices.label: D
choices.text: Movement has no effect on somatic peritoneal pain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Movement disturbs the inflamed peritoneum and worsens the pain, so patients lie still

explanation.summary: Peritonitis patients minimize movement because motion irritates the inflamed peritoneum.
explanation.whyCorrect: In peritonitis, any movement jostles the inflamed parietal peritoneum and intensifies the somatic pain, so patients lie still; colicky visceral pain (as with a stone) instead makes patients restless.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Peritonitic pain is constant and worsened by motion, not colicky or relieved by position change.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ureteral stones cause colicky visceral pain and restlessness, not peritoneal rigidity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lying still is due to pain provoked by movement, not simply weakness from hypovolemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Movement clearly aggravates somatic peritoneal pain, which is the basis for guarding and stillness.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man on CAPD is diagnosed with dialysis-associated peritonitis after his effluent turns cloudy. He remains hemodynamically stable and the catheter appears well-positioned without a tunnel infection. Which route of antibiotic administration is preferred for treating uncomplicated peritoneal dialysis peritonitis?

choices.label: C
choices.text: A single dose of intramuscular antibiotic

choices.label: D
choices.text: No antibiotics; immediate catheter removal and hemodialysis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Topical antibiotic ointment at the exit site alone

explanation.summary: Uncomplicated dialysis peritonitis is treated with intraperitoneal antibiotics via the catheter.
explanation.whyCorrect: In peritoneal dialysis peritonitis, antibiotics are instilled directly into the peritoneal cavity through the catheter, delivering high local drug concentrations to the site of infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Oral therapy alone provides inadequate peritoneal drug levels for this infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A single IM dose does not deliver sustained intraperitoneal concentrations needed for treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Catheter removal is reserved for refractory, relapsing, or fungal cases, not first-line uncomplicated bacterial peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Exit-site ointment does not treat established intraperitoneal infection.

questions.stem: A hepatologist explains that patients with cirrhotic ascites are uniquely predisposed to spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Which underlying mechanism best accounts for the development of SBP in these patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Translocation of enteric bacteria across the gut wall into ascitic fluid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct spillage of colonic contents from a perforation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Seeding of the peritoneum by metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Introduction of skin flora through an indwelling peritoneal catheter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ascending infection from the female genital tract

explanation.summary: SBP arises from bacterial translocation into ascites with weakened peritoneal defenses.
explanation.whyCorrect: In cirrhosis, enteric bacteria translocate across the intestinal wall, and the diluted, opsonin-poor ascitic fluid cannot clear them, allowing monomicrobial infection to establish without any surgical source.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Spillage from a perforation defines secondary peritonitis, not spontaneous (primary) peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metastatic seeding causes carcinomatosis with malignant ascites, not infectious SBP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Catheter-introduced skin flora describes dialysis-associated peritonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genital-tract ascending infection is a mechanism of primary peritonitis in young women but not the mechanism in cirrhotic ascites.

questions.stem: A surgical team emphasizes that antibiotics alone will not cure a patient whose peritonitis is sustained by an ongoing intra-abdominal contamination, such as a perforated sigmoid colon. The principle that a localized collection or perforation must be physically eliminated is best termed:

explanation.summary: Physically eliminating the infection source is called source control.
explanation.whyCorrect: Source control is the physical elimination of an infection focus (drainage, resection, repair, or irrigation) that antibiotics alone cannot clear; it is mandatory in secondary peritonitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antimicrobial stewardship is optimizing antibiotic use, not physically removing an infection source.
whyWrongByChoice.B: De-escalation is narrowing antibiotics after cultures, unrelated to the surgical source.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Selective gut decontamination is a prophylactic antibiotic strategy, not physical source removal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Damage-control resuscitation addresses hemorrhage/physiology, not elimination of an infectious focus.

questions.stem: A patient who required laparotomy and antibiotics for secondary peritonitis from a perforated bowel remains febrile with persistent peritoneal inflammation two weeks later. Repeat cultures grow low-virulence organisms such as Candida and coagulase-negative staphylococci, and no discrete surgically correctable source is found. Which category of peritonitis does this best represent?

explanation.summary: Persistent/recurrent peritonitis after treated secondary peritonitis with low-virulence flora is tertiary peritonitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tertiary peritonitis is persistent or recurrent intra-abdominal infection following adequately treated secondary peritonitis, typically in critically ill patients, and characteristically involves low-virulence or opportunistic organisms such as Candida and coagulase-negative staphylococci without a correctable source.

whyWrongByChoice.A: SBP occurs in cirrhotic ascites without prior surgery, not as recurrent infection after laparotomy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary peritonitis has no antecedent surgical source and is monomicrobial in cirrhotics, not this post-treatment recurrence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carcinomatosis is malignant peritoneal seeding, not an infectious recurrence with opportunistic flora.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dialysis peritonitis requires a peritoneal dialysis catheter, which this postsurgical patient does not have.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man is found to have low-grade pseudomyxoma peritonei from a ruptured mucinous appendiceal neoplasm, with mucinous deposits distributed over the peritoneal surfaces but no distant organ metastases. Which treatment approach offers the best chance of long-term control or cure?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intraperitoneal antibiotic instillation via a dialysis catheter

choices.label: C
choices.text: Emergency exploratory laparotomy for source control of infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cytoreductive surgery combined with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy

explanation.summary: Cytoreductive surgery plus HIPEC can be curative in low-grade pseudomyxoma peritonei.
explanation.whyCorrect: Complete cytoreductive (debulking) surgery combined with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) removes mucinous tumor burden and treats microscopic peritoneal disease, offering the best chance of long-term control or cure in low-grade pseudomyxoma peritonei.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pseudomyxoma peritonei is a mucinous neoplastic process, not a bacterial infection treatable with cephalosporins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intraperitoneal antibiotics treat dialysis peritonitis, not a mucinous malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Laparotomy for infectious source control does not address this noninfectious tumor; therapeutic cytoreduction plus HIPEC is required.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Observation allows progressive mucin accumulation and does not offer cure.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man presents with severe, constant epigastric pain radiating to his back, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. He drinks 8 beers daily. Which laboratory test is preferred for confirming a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis because of its superior sensitivity and specificity?

explanation.summary: Lipase is the preferred serum biomarker for diagnosing acute pancreatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serum lipase has greater sensitivity (80-100%) and specificity than amylase and stays elevated longer, making it the preferred diagnostic test for acute pancreatitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amylase is less specific because it is also elevated in salivary disease, bowel ischemia, and renal failure, so it is not preferred.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ALT suggests biliary etiology and hepatocellular injury but does not diagnose pancreatitis itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bilirubin helps identify biliary obstruction/retained stones, not the pancreatic inflammation itself.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fecal elastase-1 is a marker of chronic exocrine insufficiency, not a diagnostic test for acute pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with cholelithiasis develops acute epigastric pain and a lipase of 900 U/L. Which of the following is the single most common cause of acute pancreatitis overall?

explanation.summary: Gallstones are the most common cause of acute pancreatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gallstones account for roughly 40-70% of acute pancreatitis cases, making them the single most common etiology.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ethanol is the second most common cause (25-35%) but is less common than gallstones overall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypertriglyceridemia (TG >1,000 mg/dL) is an important but less common cause.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ERCP is a recognized iatrogenic cause but accounts for a small minority of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypercalcemia is an uncommon metabolic cause of pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A researcher studies the earliest intracellular event that triggers acute pancreatitis. Within the acinar cell, zymogen granules abnormally fuse with lysosomes, allowing a lysosomal enzyme to activate trypsinogen. Which enzyme is responsible for cleaving trypsinogen to active trypsin in this process?

explanation.summary: Cathepsin B activates trypsinogen during co-localization.
explanation.whyCorrect: When zymogen granules co-localize (fuse) with lysosomes, the lysosomal enzyme cathepsin B cleaves trypsinogen to active trypsin, initiating the autodigestive cascade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterokinase normally activates trypsinogen in the duodenal lumen, not intracellularly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Phospholipase A2 is a downstream zymogen activated by trypsin, not the initiator.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elastase is a downstream zymogen activated by trypsin, not the initiating enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Amylase is a digestive enzyme secreted normally and plays no role in trypsinogen activation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is admitted with acute pancreatitis. His triglyceride level returns at 2,400 mg/dL. Hypertriglyceridemia is generally considered a cause of acute pancreatitis when serum triglycerides exceed which threshold?

explanation.summary: Hypertriglyceridemic pancreatitis occurs above ~1,000 mg/dL.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypertriglyceridemia is considered a cause of acute pancreatitis when triglycerides exceed 1,000 mg/dL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 200 mg/dL is only borderline-high and does not cause pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 500 mg/dL is elevated but below the threshold associated with pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 750 mg/dL is elevated but still below the ~1,000 mg/dL threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 3,000 mg/dL exceeds the threshold, but the threshold at which risk begins is 1,000 mg/dL, not 3,000.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back and vomiting. Her lipase is 4x the upper limit of normal, and CT shows an edematous pancreas. According to the Revised Atlanta Criteria, how many of the three defining features are required to diagnose acute pancreatitis?

explanation.summary: Atlanta criteria require two of three features.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diagnosis requires at least two of three: characteristic abdominal pain, lipase/amylase at least 3x ULN, or characteristic cross-sectional imaging findings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One feature alone (e.g., pain only) is insufficient for diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: All three are not required; imaging is not needed if pain and enzyme criteria are met.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The criteria involve three features, not four.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The criteria involve three features, not four.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old woman is admitted with mild gallstone pancreatitis. She has no fever, hypoxia, or organ dysfunction, and her pain is controlled. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial resuscitation fluid?

explanation.summary: Lactated Ringer's is the preferred resuscitation fluid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Fluid resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's solution is the cornerstone of early acute pancreatitis management, addressing third-spacing losses of 2-4 liters over the first 48 hours.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypotonic 0.45% saline is not appropriate for volume resuscitation of third-space losses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: D5W provides free water without effective volume expansion and is not a resuscitation fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Albumin is not a first-line resuscitation fluid in acute pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: FFP is a blood product for coagulopathy, not routine volume resuscitation.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with severe acute pancreatitis develops periumbilical bluish discoloration of the skin. This finding, known as Cullen sign, most directly reflects which underlying process?

explanation.summary: Cullen sign reflects hemorrhagic pancreatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Periumbilical ecchymosis (Cullen sign) results from enzymatic destruction of blood vessels causing retroperitoneal hemorrhage that tracks to the periumbilical region, a marker of severe hemorrhagic pancreatitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Jaundice reflects biliary obstruction and causes yellow, not bluish periumbilical, discoloration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Infected necrosis causes sepsis and clinical deterioration, not periumbilical ecchymosis directly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pseudocyst formation is a late fluid collection and does not cause skin ecchymosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Splenic vein thrombosis causes gastric varices, not periumbilical discoloration.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man is hospitalized with acute pancreatitis. On day 4 his nurse asks how recovery should be monitored. Which of the following most appropriately guides tracking of his clinical improvement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Serial serum lipase levels trended daily

choices.label: B
choices.text: Degree of amylase elevation on admission

explanation.summary: Recovery is followed clinically, not by enzyme levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neither the degree nor duration of enzyme elevation correlates with severity or improvement, so recovery is followed by clinical parameters: pain control, ability to tolerate oral intake, and vital signs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Serial lipase levels do not correlate with clinical improvement and are not used to track recovery.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The degree of amylase elevation does not correlate with severity or prognosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Daily CT is unnecessary, costly, and involves excess radiation and contrast exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fecal elastase-1 assesses chronic exocrine function, not acute recovery.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man with acute pancreatitis is stable and hungry on hospital day 1 without ileus. Based on current evidence, which nutritional approach is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Strict bowel rest (NPO) until lipase normalizes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Early oral low-fat feeding within 24 hours as tolerated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nasojejunal tube feeding only, bypassing the stomach

choices.label: E
choices.text: Clear liquids only until CT confirms resolution

explanation.summary: Early oral low-fat feeding is preferred.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early oral feeding within 24 hours with a low-fat diet has replaced prolonged bowel rest, as it maintains gut integrity and reduces complications in patients who can tolerate it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Prolonged NPO until enzyme normalization is outdated; early feeding improves outcomes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TPN is reserved for those who cannot tolerate enteral nutrition and carries infection risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nasojejunal feeding is reserved for patients who cannot tolerate oral intake, not routine mild cases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Delaying feeding until imaging resolution is unnecessary and not evidence-based.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man remains ill 3 weeks after severe acute pancreatitis, with new fever, leukocytosis, and hemodynamic instability. CT shows non-enhancing pancreatic tissue with gas bubbles. Which complication best explains this late deterioration?

explanation.summary: Late deterioration with gas in necrosis indicates infected necrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infected necrosis arises when gut bacteria translocate into devitalized (non-enhancing) tissue, typically causing a mortality spike at 2-3 weeks with fever, leukocytosis, and gas on imaging.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An uncomplicated pseudocyst is a walled-off fluid collection and does not cause sepsis or gas within necrotic tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sterile edematous pancreatitis is mild and would not cause late septic deterioration with gas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chronic pancreatitis with calcification is a slow fibrotic process, not an acute septic complication.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A pseudoaneurysm causes hemorrhage, not fever with gas-containing necrosis.

questions.stem: Six weeks after an episode of acute pancreatitis, a 40-year-old man develops early satiety and a palpable epigastric mass. CT reveals a round, amylase-rich peripancreatic fluid collection posterior to the pancreatic tail with a thick non-epithelial wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A walled-off amylase-rich collection without epithelial lining is a pseudocyst.
explanation.whyCorrect: A pseudocyst is a walled-off, amylase-rich peripancreatic fluid collection whose wall is fibrous/inflammatory rather than epithelial ('pseudo'), typically forming several weeks after acute pancreatitis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A true cyst has an epithelial lining, whereas this collection has a fibroinflammatory wall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An abscess implies infection with pus and systemic signs, not described here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A mucinous cystic neoplasm has an epithelial (ovarian-type stroma) lining and is unrelated to a recent pancreatitis episode.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adenocarcinoma is a solid mass, not an amylase-rich fluid collection.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with gallstone pancreatitis has a rising total bilirubin and a common bile duct measuring 11 mm on ultrasound. Which finding most strongly indicates a retained obstructing stone requiring ERCP with stone extraction?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rising bilirubin with a dilated common bile duct

explanation.summary: Rising bilirubin plus a dilated CBD predicts a retained stone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Elevated or rising bilirubin combined with a dilated common bile duct (>=9 mm) strongly predicts a retained obstructing stone, indicating a need for ERCP with extraction (required in ~15% of gallstone pancreatitis).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lipase confirms pancreatitis but does not indicate a retained stone; most gallstones pass spontaneously.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Low fecal elastase reflects chronic exocrine insufficiency, unrelated to acute biliary obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elevated triglycerides suggest a different (metabolic) etiology, not a retained biliary stone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leukocytosis is nonspecific and may reflect the inflammatory response alone.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with a long history of heavy alcohol use has recurrent epigastric pain over 2 years. Serum amylase and lipase are normal, but CT shows an atrophic pancreas with diffuse calcifications. Which imaging finding is considered virtually pathognomonic for chronic pancreatitis?

explanation.summary: Calcifications are nearly pathognomonic for chronic pancreatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pancreatic calcifications are the hallmark imaging finding of established chronic pancreatitis, with nearly 100% specificity; about 85% of advanced alcohol-induced cases show them.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Peripancreatic fluid collections are a feature of acute pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Non-enhancing necrotic parenchyma indicates acute necrotizing pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A dilated CBD suggests biliary obstruction, not specifically chronic pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A pseudocyst can occur in either form and is not specific for chronic disease.

questions.stem: A researcher studies fibrogenesis in chronic pancreatitis. Which cell, when activated, transforms into a collagen-producing myofibroblast and represents the final common pathway of pancreatic fibrosis?

explanation.summary: The stellate cell drives chronic pancreatitis fibrosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pancreatic stellate cells are the key cell of chronic pancreatitis; upon activation by cytokines (TGF-beta, PDGF), they lose their vitamin A stores and transform into collagen-depositing myofibroblasts, the final common pathway of fibrogenesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The acinar cell is central to acute pancreatitis (enzyme activation), not the fibrogenic cell of chronic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Islet beta cells produce insulin and are destroyed in the process, but they do not deposit collagen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ductal epithelial cells contribute to secretion but are not the collagen-producing fibrogenic cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Kupffer cells are hepatic macrophages, not pancreatic fibrogenic cells.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis reports bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools that float. This steatorrhea from fat malabsorption typically does not appear until what proportion of exocrine function has been lost?

explanation.summary: Steatorrhea appears after >90% exocrine loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the pancreas has enormous functional reserve, clinically significant steatorrhea generally does not appear until more than 90% of exocrine function is lost.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of >25% is well within the gland's reserve and does not cause steatorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of >50% still leaves adequate enzyme output to prevent steatorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of >75% is still below the ~90% threshold needed for clinically evident steatorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Small losses are compensated by the large reserve of enzyme secretion.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with alcoholic chronic pancreatitis develops new hyperglycemia and, on one occasion, prolonged hypoglycemia after insulin. His pancreatogenic (type 3c) diabetes differs from type 1 and type 2 diabetes because it results from:

choices.label: C
choices.text: Excess glucagon secretion from an alpha-cell tumor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of both beta cells and alpha cells

explanation.summary: Type 3c diabetes destroys both beta and alpha cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type 3c (pancreatogenic) diabetes arises from destruction of pancreatic endocrine tissue including both insulin-producing beta cells and glucagon-producing alpha cells, causing brittle glucose control with a tendency to hypoglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction alone describes type 1 diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Peripheral insulin resistance describes type 2 diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Excess glucagon from a tumor describes a glucagonoma, not type 3c diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Insulin receptor antibodies describe rare type B insulin resistance, not pancreatogenic diabetes.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with established chronic pancreatitis continues to drink alcohol and smoke. Which intervention is the single most important step to slow disease progression?

explanation.summary: Cessation of alcohol and smoking is the most important intervention.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alcohol and smoking each independently drive disease progression, so cessation of both is the single most important intervention in chronic pancreatitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enzyme replacement treats exocrine insufficiency symptoms but does not halt progression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin manages endocrine insufficiency but does not slow the fibrotic process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endoscopic stone removal addresses ductal obstruction/pain but is not the most important progression-modifying step.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prophylactic antibiotics have no role in slowing chronic pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with chronic pancreatitis and steatorrhea is prescribed pancrelipase. To achieve effective digestion, pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy should be taken:

choices.label: A
choices.text: On an empty stomach at bedtime

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only once daily in the morning

explanation.summary: Pancrelipase must be taken with meals.
explanation.whyCorrect: Taking pancrelipase with meals (and snacks) synchronizes enzyme delivery with the arriving chyme, restoring digestion; lipase is the key component.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Taking it on an empty stomach at bedtime provides no substrate to digest and wastes the enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Once-daily dosing fails to cover other meals and leaves food undigested.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dosing two hours after eating misses the meal it is meant to digest.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancrelipase is an oral formulation; it is not given intravenously.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man has three episodes of acute pancreatitis over 4 years despite no identifiable ongoing insult. His physician counsels him about long-term risk. Recurrent acute pancreatitis is significant primarily because it is the strongest risk factor for:

explanation.summary: Recurrent acute pancreatitis predisposes to chronic pancreatitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recurrent acute pancreatitis is the strongest risk factor for chronic pancreatitis; about one-third of patients with recurrent acute pancreatitis progress to chronic disease.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A glucagonoma is a neuroendocrine tumor unrelated to recurrent pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autoimmune hepatitis is a distinct liver disease, not caused by recurrent pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary sclerosing cholangitis affects bile ducts and is associated with IBD, not recurrent pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gilbert syndrome is an inherited bilirubin conjugation defect unrelated to pancreatitis.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with intractable pain from chronic pancreatitis has a dilated, obstructed main pancreatic duct with strictures and stones on imaging. Serum enzymes are normal. Which of the following is a treatment specifically aimed at his chronic pancreatitis?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aggressive resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's for third-spacing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endoscopic dilation and drainage of the pancreatic duct

explanation.summary: Ductal decompression treats refractory chronic pancreatitis pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Endoscopic dilation/stenting (or surgical drainage such as a lateral pancreaticojejunostomy) relieves ductal obstruction and treats refractory pain in chronic pancreatitis with a dilated, obstructed duct.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholecystectomy treats gallstone-related acute pancreatitis, not obstructive chronic pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ICU management of MODS applies to severe acute pancreatitis, not chronic ductal disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Third-spacing resuscitation is a feature of acute pancreatitis management.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antibiotics target infected necrosis in acute pancreatitis, not chronic ductal obstruction.

questions.stem: A 73-year-old man presents with 2 months of fatigue, a 15-lb weight loss, and yellowing of the skin and sclera noted by his wife. He has a 20-pack-year smoking history. Physical exam is notable only for jaundice. Laboratory studies show a conjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Which pancreatic tumor location best explains this clinical picture?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Uncinate process extending into the spleen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Diffuse involvement of the pancreatic tail and hilum

explanation.summary: Painless jaundice from bile duct obstruction points to a head-of-pancreas tumor.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 75% of pancreatic adenocarcinomas arise in the head or neck of the pancreas. A mass here obstructs the common bile duct, producing conjugated (obstructive) hyperbilirubinemia and jaundice, exactly as seen in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Tail tumors do not compress the common bile duct and typically present late with pain or metastases rather than early jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Body tumors more often cause epigastric or back pain and do not commonly obstruct the bile duct to produce painless jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The uncinate process does not extend to the spleen, and this location is not the typical explanation for bile duct obstruction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Diffuse tail involvement would not obstruct the common bile duct and would not present primarily with obstructive jaundice.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with a newly diagnosed pancreatic mass is found on examination to have a palpably enlarged, nontender gallbladder together with mild painless jaundice. Which eponymous sign does this finding represent?

explanation.summary: A nontender enlarged gallbladder with painless jaundice is the Courvoisier sign.
explanation.whyCorrect: Courvoisier sign is a palpably enlarged, nontender gallbladder accompanied by mild painless jaundice, classically caused by malignant obstruction of the distal common bile duct such as a pancreatic head carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Trousseau sign refers to migratory thrombophlebitis, not a palpable gallbladder.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Murphy sign is inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation, seen in acute cholecystitis, and is associated with a tender gallbladder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Virchow node is a left supraclavicular lymph node from metastatic abdominal malignancy, not a gallbladder finding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sister Mary Joseph nodule is a periumbilical metastatic nodule, not an enlarged gallbladder.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with pancreatic adenocarcinoma develops recurrent, migrating episodes of superficial venous thrombosis affecting different sites over several weeks. This paraneoplastic phenomenon is attributed to procoagulants such as tissue factor and mucins released by the tumor. What is this sign called?

explanation.summary: Migratory thrombophlebitis in malignancy is the Trousseau sign.
explanation.whyCorrect: Trousseau sign is migratory thrombophlebitis caused by platelet-activating factors and procoagulants (tissue factor and mucins) released by the carcinoma, and it is classically associated with pancreatic cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Courvoisier sign is a palpable nontender gallbladder with painless jaundice, not migratory thrombophlebitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Double-duct sign is an imaging finding of dilated bile and pancreatic ducts, not a coagulation phenomenon.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Homans sign is calf discomfort on dorsiflexion suggesting deep venous thrombosis, not migratory superficial thrombophlebitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cullen sign is periumbilical bruising seen in hemorrhagic pancreatitis, not a hypercoagulable phenomenon.

questions.stem: A pathologist reviews a core biopsy of a firm pancreatic head mass. Which microscopic feature is most characteristic of infiltrating pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Malignant glands haphazardly arranged within a dense collagenous stroma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sheets of monotonous neuroendocrine cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Well-delineated cysts lined by ciliated epithelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clusters of signet ring cells filling the lamina propria

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nests of clear cells with abundant glycogen

explanation.summary: Ductal adenocarcinoma shows malignant glands in desmoplastic stroma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infiltrating ductal adenocarcinoma is characterized by malignant glands arranged haphazardly within a dense desmoplastic (collagenous) stroma, frequently with perineural and vascular invasion.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sheets of cells with salt-and-pepper chromatin describe a neuroendocrine tumor, which is a distinct and far less common pancreatic malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cysts lined by ciliated epithelium are not a feature of ductal adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Signet ring cells are typical of certain gastric or colonic carcinomas, not the defining feature of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Clear cells rich in glycogen suggest renal cell carcinoma, not pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: In the stepwise molecular progression of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, which gene alteration is considered the initiating event and is present in nearly all cases?

explanation.summary: KRAS activation is the first and near-universal driver mutation.
explanation.whyCorrect: An activating KRAS mutation on chromosome 12p occurs in almost all cases and is the first step in the stepwise progression to pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: p16 inactivation occurs after KRAS activation (in ~95% of cases) and is not the initiating event.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p53 inactivation occurs later in the sequence, in 50%-75% of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: DPC4/SMAD4 loss is a late event occurring in ~55% of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HER2 is overexpressed in about 50% of cases but is not the initiating driver mutation.

questions.stem: A researcher studies the earliest oncogenic driver in pancreatic cancer. The mutated protein is a GTPase that normally inactivates itself by hydrolyzing GTP to GDP but, when mutated, remains locked in its active form. Which is the normal function that is lost with this mutation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibition of the G1-to-S cell cycle transition

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intrinsic GTPase activity that converts GTP to GDP

explanation.summary: Mutant KRAS loses its intrinsic GTPase (self-inactivating) activity.
explanation.whyCorrect: KRAS is active when GTP-bound; its intrinsic GTPase activity normally hydrolyzes GTP to GDP to switch it off. The activating mutation disrupts this GTPase activity, locking KRAS in the active GTP-bound state and driving continuous growth signaling.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Inhibiting the G1-to-S transition is the function of p16, a tumor suppressor, not KRAS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Triggering apoptosis after DNA damage describes p53, not KRAS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting TGF-dependent development is the role of DPC4/SMAD4, not KRAS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mismatch repair is performed by Lynch syndrome genes (MLH1, MSH2), not KRAS.

questions.stem: A tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 18q, whose name reflects that it is 'Deleted in Pancreatic Cancer,' is important for inhibiting TGF-reliant cellular development and is lost in roughly 55% of pancreatic adenocarcinomas. Which gene is this?

explanation.summary: DPC4/SMAD4 on 18q is lost in ~55% of cases and inhibits TGF signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: DPC4/SMAD4 (Deleted in Pancreatic Cancer, locus 4) is a tumor suppressor on chromosome 18q that inhibits TGF-reliant cellular development; it is lost in about 55% of pancreatic adenocarcinomas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: KRAS is an oncogene on chromosome 12p activated in nearly all cases, not a TGF-pathway tumor suppressor on 18q.
whyWrongByChoice.B: p16 is on chromosome 9p and inhibits the G1-to-S transition, not the TGF pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p53 is on chromosome 17p and governs cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis after DNA damage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: STK11 is the Peutz-Jeghers gene, not the chromosome 18q gene described here.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man is diagnosed with pancreatic adenocarcinoma. His oncologist orders a serum tumor marker. Which statement about the appropriate marker is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CA 19-9 is used primarily to establish the initial diagnosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5-HIAA is the marker of choice for pancreatic adenocarcinoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: CA 19-9 is used mainly for prognosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: CA 125 is the specific marker for pancreatic adenocarcinoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Alpha-fetoprotein is the standard marker for pancreatic adenocarcinoma

explanation.summary: CA 19-9 is a prognostic, not diagnostic, marker.
explanation.whyCorrect: CA 19-9 is the tumor marker associated with pancreatic cancer and is used mainly for prognosis rather than diagnosis; lower levels indicate a better prognosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CA 19-9 is not used to establish the initial diagnosis; it is chiefly prognostic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 5-HIAA is a urinary marker for carcinoid (serotonin-secreting) tumors, not pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CA 125 is associated with ovarian cancer, not pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha-fetoprotein is elevated in hepatocellular carcinoma and germ cell tumors, not pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with weight loss undergoes contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen. The radiologist reports simultaneous dilation of the common bile duct and the main pancreatic duct. This 'double-duct sign' is most suggestive of which condition?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma of the head

explanation.summary: The double-duct sign points to a head-of-pancreas carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The double-duct sign is dilation of both the common bile duct and the pancreatic duct on contrast-enhanced CT, produced by a pancreatic head carcinoma obstructing both ducts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic pancreatitis can cause ductal changes but the double-duct sign in this setting strongly raises concern for an obstructing malignancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A cystic duct stone obstructs the gallbladder outflow and does not produce combined bile and pancreatic duct dilation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A duplicated IVC is a vascular anomaly unrelated to ductal dilation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A hepatic artery aneurysm is a vascular finding, not a cause of paired ductal dilation.

questions.stem: A medical student reviews epidemiology of pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Which single modifiable risk factor is described as one of the most important, roughly doubling the risk of the disease?

explanation.summary: Smoking nearly doubles pancreatic cancer risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cigarette smoking is one of the most important risk factors and nearly doubles (roughly 2x) the risk of pancreatic carcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: While diet is discussed as a general factor, processed meats are not the factor described as roughly doubling the risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Moderate alcohol use is not cited as the factor that doubles risk; chronic pancreatitis and smoking are emphasized instead.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sedentary lifestyle alone is not identified as the key doubling risk factor; obesity is a listed contributor but smoking is the emphasized one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Caffeine intake is not identified as a significant risk factor for pancreatic carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has a strong family history of breast and ovarian cancer and is found to carry a germline BRCA2 mutation. Beyond breast and ovarian cancer, this inherited syndrome increases her risk of which of the following?

explanation.summary: BRCA1/2 mutations raise pancreatic adenocarcinoma risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hereditary breast/ovarian cancer syndrome (BRCA1, BRCA2) is among the inherited syndromes that raise the risk of pancreatic adenocarcinoma; inherited syndromes account for about 10% of patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is associated with MEN2/RET mutations, not BRCA2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pheochromocytoma is linked to MEN2, VHL, and neurofibromatosis, not BRCA2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Osteosarcoma is associated with Li-Fraumeni (TP53) and hereditary retinoblastoma, not BRCA2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retinoblastoma is caused by RB1 mutations, not BRCA2.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with abdominal complaints and STK11 (LKB1) mutation has mucocutaneous pigmentation of the lips and multiple hamartomatous GI polyps. Which pancreatic-related risk does this syndrome confer, and what is its name?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, with increased pancreatic neuroendocrine risk only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Familial pancreatitis, from a PRSS1 mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, with increased risk of pancreatic adenocarcinoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hereditary breast/ovarian cancer, from a BRCA1 mutation

explanation.summary: STK11 with pigmentation and hamartomas is Peutz-Jeghers, which raises pancreatic cancer risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is caused by STK11 mutations and is one of the inherited syndromes that increases the risk of pancreatic adenocarcinoma; it features mucocutaneous pigmentation and hamartomatous polyps.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Von Hippel-Lindau is caused by VHL mutations, not STK11, and does not present with mucocutaneous pigmentation and hamartomatous polyps.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lynch syndrome results from mismatch-repair genes such as MLH1 or MSH2, not STK11.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Familial pancreatitis is caused by PRSS1 mutations, not STK11, and lacks the mucocutaneous pigmentation described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hereditary breast/ovarian cancer is caused by BRCA1/BRCA2, not STK11.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man is diagnosed with a resectable adenocarcinoma confined to the head of the pancreas with no distant spread. Which surgical procedure is the standard operation for a tumor in this location?

explanation.summary: Head-of-pancreas tumors are resected by the Whipple procedure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pancreaticoduodenectomy (the Whipple procedure) is the standard resection for a tumor localized to the head of the pancreas, removing the pancreatic head, duodenum, and adjacent structures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy is used for tumors of the body or tail, not the head.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Total gastrectomy is an operation for gastric cancer, not pancreatic head carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Left hepatectomy removes liver, which is not the primary resection for a localized pancreatic head tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass is a bariatric/anatomic bypass operation, not a cancer resection.

questions.stem: At the time of diagnosis, what proportion of patients with pancreatic adenocarcinoma have disease that has already spread beyond the pancreas, and what is the therapeutic implication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fewer than 20%; most are candidates for curative resection

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 40%; the majority undergo curative surgery

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 60%; radiation alone is usually curative

choices.label: D
choices.text: More than 80%; management is often largely palliative

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nearly 100%; all patients undergo liver transplantation

explanation.summary: Over 80% present with spread, so care is often palliative.
explanation.whyCorrect: More than 80% of cases have already spread beyond the pancreas at diagnosis; because most cases are advanced, management is largely palliative and focused on symptom relief.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only a minority present with localized, resectable disease; the majority have already spread.
whyWrongByChoice.B: About 40% is an underestimate; more than 80% have spread by diagnosis and most do not undergo curative surgery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Radiation alone is not curative for pancreatic adenocarcinoma, and the fraction with spread is higher than 60%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Liver transplantation is not a standard treatment for pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man asks about his prognosis after being diagnosed with pancreatic cancer that is localized and has not spread outside the pancreas. Compared with the poor overall outlook, what is the approximate 5-year survival for localized disease?

explanation.summary: Localized pancreatic cancer has a ~37.4% 5-year survival.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early, pre-spread (localized) diagnosis raises the 5-year survival to about 37.4%, substantially higher than the overall rate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 9.3% is the overall 5-year survival across all stages, not the localized rate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 75% overstates the localized survival for pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 90% is far higher than the reported localized survival of ~37.4%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 1% dramatically understates even the poor overall survival of ~9.3%.

questions.stem: A student compares the two broad categories of pancreatic tumors. Which statement correctly distinguishes pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma from pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (NETs)?

choices.label: A
choices.text: NETs make up about 85% of pancreatic tumors and arise from ductal cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adenocarcinoma arises from islet cells, whereas NETs arise from ductal cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adenocarcinoma is the rarer of the two and is usually slow-growing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both adenocarcinoma and NETs arise from the endocrine pancreas

choices.label: E
choices.text: NETs are less than 5% of pancreatic tumors, arise from hormone-producing islet cells, and are often nonfunctional and slow-growing

explanation.summary: NETs are <5% of pancreatic tumors, arise from islet cells, and are often indolent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors constitute less than 5% of pancreatic tumors, arise from hormone-producing islet cells of the endocrine pancreas, and are frequently nonfunctional and slow-growing, in contrast with the aggressive ductal adenocarcinoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenocarcinoma, not NETs, makes up about 85% of pancreatic carcinomas and arises from ductal cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This reverses the origins: adenocarcinoma arises from ductal (exocrine) cells and NETs from islet (endocrine) cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adenocarcinoma is the more common and more aggressive tumor, not the rarer or slow-growing one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adenocarcinoma arises from the exocrine (ductal/acinar) pancreas, not the endocrine pancreas.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman presents with episodic weakness, sweating, palpitations, and confusion that resolve after eating. Fasting studies show hypoglycemia with inappropriately elevated insulin. Which pancreatic tumor is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ductal adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head

explanation.summary: Fasting hypoglycemia with high insulin indicates an insulinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulinoma is the most common pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor and produces hypoglycemia with weakness and sweating due to inappropriate insulin secretion, matching this presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ductal adenocarcinoma typically causes painless jaundice, weight loss, and pain, not hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mucinous cystadenocarcinoma is a cystic exocrine neoplasm and does not secrete insulin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastrinoma causes refractory peptic ulcers and diarrhea from excess gastrin (Zollinger-Ellison), not hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acinar cell carcinoma is a rare exocrine tumor and does not classically cause hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old previously healthy man develops new-onset diabetes mellitus, followed within months by epigastric gnawing pain and weight loss. His physician is concerned this diabetes may be a presenting sign of malignancy. Which pancreatic condition is most consistent with this constellation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Type 1 diabetes mellitus from autoimmune islet destruction

explanation.summary: Sudden new diabetes with pain and weight loss can herald pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sudden-onset new diabetes mellitus is listed among the clinical signs and symptoms of pancreatic adenocarcinoma, and here it is accompanied by epigastric gnawing pain and weight loss, a classic presenting constellation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Type 1 diabetes typically presents in younger patients with autoimmune islet destruction and is not accompanied by this cancer-associated pain and weight loss.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Simple obesity-related type 2 diabetes develops gradually and does not explain the acute pain and significant weight loss seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemochromatosis causes 'bronze diabetes' with iron overload features, not acute epigastric pain and weight loss suggestive of a mass.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gestational diabetes occurs in pregnancy and is unrelated to this older male patient.

questions.stem: A pathologist notes that malignant glands in a pancreatic adenocarcinoma specimen are tracking along and wrapping around adjacent nerves. This feature is common in pancreatic cancer and provides a route for spread outside the pancreas. What is it called?

explanation.summary: Tumor tracking along nerves is perineural invasion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Perineural invasion is the spread of malignant glands along nerves, a common feature of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma that provides a route for the cancer to spread outside the pancreas.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphovascular invasion is spread through lymphatics or blood vessels, not along nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metaplasia is a reversible change of one differentiated cell type to another, not invasion along nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Desmoplasia is the dense collagenous stroma produced around the tumor, not spread along nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dysplasia refers to disordered but pre-invasive epithelial growth, not nerve invasion.

questions.stem: During autopsy review of patients who died of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, which set of organs represents the most common sites of metastatic spread?

explanation.summary: Pancreatic cancer most often spreads to lungs, liver, and peritoneum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most common metastasis sites for pancreatic adenocarcinoma are the lungs, liver, and peritoneum.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Brain, adrenal, and thyroid are not the characteristic metastatic sites for pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone, prostate, and skin are not the typical pattern of pancreatic cancer spread.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Kidney, spleen, and heart are uncommon sites for pancreatic cancer metastasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The reproductive organs are not the common metastatic destinations for pancreatic adenocarcinoma.

questions.topicName: Exocrine Functions of the GI System
questions.stem: A physiology student examines a section of jejunal mucosa under the microscope and notes numerous finger-like mucosal projections, each containing a core capillary network and a central lacteal, that together increase the absorptive surface area roughly 10-fold. Which structure is being described?

explanation.summary: Villi are the finger-like projections, each with a capillary network and central lacteal, that add roughly a 10-fold amplification of small intestinal surface area.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that villi project from the plicae and add another ~10-fold amplification, and that each villus core contains a capillary network and a central lacteal that drains absorbed lipids into the lymphatics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Plicae circulares are permanent circular folds (most prominent in the jejunum) that add only about a 3-fold increase, not the finger-like projections described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Microvilli form the brush border on the apical enterocyte surface and add ~20-fold amplification; they are not visible finger-like mucosal projections with lacteals.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Crypts of Lieberkühn house progenitor cells for epithelial renewal, not the absorptive projections described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Brush border enzymes are membrane proteins that complete terminal digestion; they are not a structural surface-amplifying projection.

questions.topicName: Exocrine Functions of the GI System
questions.stem: A researcher analyzes fresh pancreatic juice and finds that most proteolytic components are catalytically inactive precursors, but two components are already enzymatically active on secretion. Which pair is normally secreted in the active form?

explanation.summary: Pancreatic amylase and lipase are secreted in active form and do not require luminal activation, unlike the proteases secreted as zymogens.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explicitly states that pancreatic lipase and amylase are secreted in active form and do not require luminal activation, whereas proteases are secreted as inactive zymogens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Trypsinogen and chymotrypsinogen are inactive zymogens requiring activation in the duodenum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Proelastase and procolipase are inactive precursors activated by trypsin in the lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Procarboxypeptidases A and B are zymogens requiring trypsin-mediated activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Prophospholipase A2 and proelastase are both inactive precursors, not active enzymes.

questions.topicName: Exocrine Functions of the GI System
questions.stem: A biochemistry question focuses on the committed, rate-limiting step by which hepatocytes convert cholesterol into primary bile acids. Which enzyme catalyzes this rate-limiting step?

explanation.summary: Cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase (CYP7A1) is the rate-limiting enzyme of de novo bile acid synthesis from cholesterol in hepatocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that primary bile acids are synthesized de novo in hepatocytes from cholesterol via a multi-step pathway in which the rate-limiting enzyme is cholesterol 7α-hydroxylase (CYP7A1).

whyWrongByChoice.B: HMG-CoA reductase is the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis, not of bile acid synthesis from cholesterol.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carbonic anhydrase generates bicarbonate in pancreatic duct cells and has no role in bile acid synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen in the duodenum and is unrelated to bile acid synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pancreatic lipase hydrolyzes dietary triglycerides and does not synthesize bile acids.

questions.topicName: Exocrine Functions of the GI System
questions.stem: In the duodenal lumen, the pancreatic protease activation cascade must be initiated. Which duodenal brush border enzyme converts trypsinogen to trypsin to start this cascade?

explanation.summary: Enteropeptidase (enterokinase), a duodenal brush border enzyme, cleaves trypsinogen to generate active trypsin and initiate the cascade.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states the cascade is initiated by enteropeptidase (historically enterokinase), a brush border enzyme of duodenal enterocytes that cleaves a hexapeptide from trypsinogen to generate active trypsin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chymotrypsin is itself a downstream product of trypsin activation and does not initiate the cascade.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Colipase is a lipase cofactor, not an activator of trypsinogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Carboxypeptidase A is a zymogen product of the cascade, not its initiator.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Amylase digests starch and plays no role in zymogen activation.

questions.topicName: Exocrine Functions of the GI System
questions.stem: Once the first active protease is generated in the duodenum, it proceeds to cleave and activate the remaining pancreatic zymogens as well as additional molecules of its own precursor. Which enzyme serves as this master activator?

explanation.summary: Trypsin is the master activator that cleaves and activates the other pancreatic zymogens and additional trypsinogen (autocatalytic amplification).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states trypsin acts as the master activator of the cascade, cleaving and activating all other pancreatic zymogens plus additional trypsinogen molecules.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Enteropeptidase only activates trypsinogen to trypsin; it does not activate the other zymogens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chymotrypsin is a product of trypsin-mediated activation, not the master activator.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elastase is generated from proelastase by trypsin and does not activate other zymogens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Carboxypeptidase A is a downstream product and does not drive the cascade.

questions.topicName: Exocrine Functions of the GI System
questions.stem: Pancreatic duct cells generate a bicarbonate-rich fluid using a key apical transport protein whose loss underlies cystic fibrosis. This protein functions as which type of channel?

explanation.summary: CFTR on the apical membrane of pancreatic duct cells is a cAMP-activated chloride channel central to bicarbonate secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies the key transporter as the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR), a cAMP-activated chloride channel located on the apical membrane of duct cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) mediates intestinal glucose uptake, not ductal chloride secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ATP-gated potassium channels regulate insulin release in beta cells, not ductal bicarbonate output.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Voltage-gated calcium channels mediate depolarization-triggered signaling, not CFTR function.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CFTR is regulated by cAMP, not by direct ligand gating of a sodium channel.

questions.topicName: Exocrine Functions of the GI System
questions.stem: Following a meal, acid chyme enters the duodenum, triggering hormone release from duodenal S cells. This hormone acts primarily to promote which secretion?

explanation.summary: Secretin, released from duodenal S cells in response to luminal acid, primarily stimulates duct cells to secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states secretin is released from S cells in response to luminal acid and primarily stimulates duct cells to secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enzyme secretion from acinar cells is primarily driven by CCK, not secretin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Secretin does not stimulate parietal cell acid secretion; it opposes gastric acidity by promoting neutralization.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Goblet cell mucus secretion is not the primary secretin-driven response described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intrinsic factor secretion is unrelated to secretin signaling.

questions.topicName: Exocrine Functions of the GI System
questions.stem: When a fatty, protein-rich meal reaches the duodenum, I cells release a hormone that promotes gallbladder contraction and pancreatic secretion. This hormone primarily stimulates which secretion?

explanation.summary: CCK, released from duodenal I cells in response to luminal fats and proteins, primarily stimulates acinar cells to secrete digestive enzymes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states CCK is released from I cells in response to luminal fats and proteins and primarily stimulates acinar cells to secrete digestive enzymes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bicarbonate secretion by duct cells is primarily driven by secretin, not CCK.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Parietal cell acid secretion is not the primary CCK-driven pancreatic response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Goblet cell mucus secretion is not the described CCK effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Intrinsic factor secretion is unrelated to CCK signaling.

questions.topicName: Exocrine Functions of the GI System
questions.stem: A question asks students to identify the two primary bile acids that are synthesized de novo in hepatocytes directly from cholesterol. Which pair is correct?

explanation.summary: Cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid are the primary bile acids synthesized de novo in hepatocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states the primary bile acids are cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid, synthesized de novo in hepatocytes from cholesterol.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deoxycholic and lithocholic acid are secondary bile acids produced by colonic bacteria, not primary.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ursodeoxycholic acid is not one of the two primary bile acids described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lithocholic acid is a secondary bile acid, so this pair is incorrect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Deoxycholic acid is a secondary bile acid, so this pair is incorrect.

questions.topicName: Exocrine Functions of the GI System
questions.stem: In the colon, intestinal bacteria deconjugate and dehydroxylate primary bile acids to generate secondary bile acids that can be reabsorbed and recycled. Which pair represents these secondary bile acids?

explanation.summary: Deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid are the secondary bile acids formed by colonic bacterial modification of primary bile acids.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that colonic bacteria deconjugate and dehydroxylate primary bile acids to produce the secondary bile acids deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholic and chenodeoxycholic acid are the primary bile acids, not secondary.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glycocholic and taurocholic acid are conjugated forms of primary bile acids, not bacterial secondary products.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This pair includes cholic acid (a primary bile acid), so it is incorrect.
